analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and Europe.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to write rules allowing wholesale distributors, pharmacies, and individuals to import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and European Union countries, where the same drugs often sell for far less. It expands eligibility to include biologics such as insulin, lets individuals fill U.S. prescriptions at certified foreign pharmacies for up to a 90-day supply, bans manufacturers from charging foreign sellers more or cutting off their supply, and adds criminal penalties for websites selling counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a prescription.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who skip or ration prescriptions because of cost. The bill's own findings cite studies showing tens of millions of Americans have declined to fill a prescription due to price, and note U.S. drug prices average 2.78 times those of comparable countries. Individuals could buy a 90-day supply directly from a certified foreign pharmacy, and U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers could import qualifying drugs, including insulin and biologics. People who currently import for personal use under waivers or enforcement discretion would get a clear legal pathway instead of risking seizure at the border.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to issue regulations within one year permitting importation of qualifying drugs from Canada, the UK, EU member states, and Switzerland, and removes the certification requirement that HHS used for years to block importation.
Expands eligible drugs to include biologics such as insulin, peritoneal dialysis solution, and intravenously infused drugs, categories excluded from current law.
Lets individuals use a certified licensed foreign pharmacy to fill a U.S. prescription for up to a 90-day personal supply, replacing the current waiver system.

Makes it illegal for manufacturers to charge foreign sellers more than domestic buyers, deny or delay supply to certified sellers, or make the U.S. version of a drug differ from the exported version to defeat importation.

Adds criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison or a $250,000 fine for websites selling counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a valid prescription, and requires quality testing, seller certification, recall notification, and suspension authority for noncompliant sellers.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose ability to sustain much higher U.S. prices depends on keeping cheaper identical foreign versions out. The bill's findings state U.S. prices are on average 2.78 times those of comparable countries and 4.22 times higher for patented drugs. Manufacturers would face anti-discrimination rules barring them from overcharging or restricting supply to certified foreign sellers. Foreign pharmacies and distributors would pay certification fees and meet testing and compliance obligations.

drawbacks.text: Federal health officials long declined to certify importation under existing law, citing safety concerns such as contamination and counterfeiting; this bill removes that certification requirement entirely, relying instead on seller certification, testing, and suspension authority to catch problems after importation begins.

The bill's effectiveness depends on manufacturers not finding ways around the anti-discrimination rules; it tries to prevent supply restrictions and price discrimination against certified sellers, but how enforceable those bans prove in practice is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who skip prescriptions over cost, the potential gain is large and direct: a legal route to the same drugs at foreign prices, with insulin and biologics included. The main honest concern is safety, since the certification requirement that guarded against contaminated or counterfeit imports would be replaced by a certification-and-testing regime that has not been operated. The bill does include real safeguards — approved labs, random testing, recall duties, suspension power, and new criminal penalties for counterfeit sellers — so the trade-off is a bet that oversight can match what certification provided, in exchange for price competition that current law has never delivered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 1, 2025, joined by Reps. Cohen, Doggett, Omar, Pingree, and Pocan.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only action taken on it.
Eight House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republicans have.

Current law lets HHS authorize importation only from Canada and only after certifying it poses no additional safety risk; HHS declined for years on safety grounds before certifying in 2020, and only one state plan has been approved since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything and nothing has changed: brand-name drug manufacturers keep the status quo in which the same drugs sell for 2.78 times more in the United States than abroad, and patients keep paying those prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers keep the status quo

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on May 1, 2025 — no hearing, markup, or floor scheduling.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have consistently lobbied against prescription drug importation legislation, arguing it threatens drug safety and undermines investment in new medicines.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters (sponsor plus cosponsors) are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; no vote has occurred, so no roll-call picture exists.

industries.note: Importation would expose U.S. patients to the same drugs sold abroad at a fraction of U.S. prices — the bill's findings put the gap at 2.78 times overall and 4.22 times for patented drugs. The bill also bans manufacturers from overcharging or cutting supply to certified foreign sellers, directly attacking the pricing structure that keeps U.S. prices high.

industries.industry: Licensed foreign pharmacies and wholesale distributors (Canada, UK, EU, Switzerland)
industries.note: A new certified-seller program would open a U.S. customer base for these pharmacies and distributors, in exchange for certification fees, quality testing, recall duties, and English labeling. Their gain — selling the same drug to Americans at the price they charge at home — comes directly out of drug makers' U.S. margins, not patients' pockets.

Registered U.S. dispensers and wholesalers could become importers and buy qualifying drugs at foreign prices, but they would also face new competition from individuals buying directly from certified foreign pharmacies.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a partisan Democratic proposal with only 8 cosponsors sitting on a committee that has shown no interest in it. Similar importation bills have repeatedly stalled in committee in past Congresses; the most likely path is that it dies without a markup or vote when this Congress ends in January 2027.
